Status: accepted

Amends decisions 3, 4 and 5, and adds decision 16.

## Context

Corium ships one Kubernetes version per OS image. `build/k0s.lock` pins a release
and two checksums, `build/scripts/install-k0s.sh` fetches it into `/usr/bin/k0s`
at build time, and decision 3 states the rule that makes this deliberate rather
than incidental: the binary is image-owned, replaced wholesale on upgrade, never
written at runtime. Decision 4 follows from it — a Kubernetes upgrade is a new
image, `bootc upgrade`, a reboot, and an atomic rollback if it goes wrong. One
upgrade mechanism, one version axis, free rollback.

That is a good trade for the OS. It is a bad trade for Kubernetes, because the two
things move for different reasons and at different rates.

An operator on Corium 0.3.6 runs Kubernetes 1.36.4 because that is what 0.3.6
contains. To reach 1.37 they wait for a Corium release that carries it. To take a
Fedora security fix they take whatever Kubernetes minor that Corium release
happens to carry, whether or not their workloads are ready for it. Neither
direction is separable today, and both are ordinary requests. The coupling also
lands on the project: every Kubernetes minor Corium wants to offer is a Corium
release, and every Corium release is a statement about a Kubernetes version it did
not intend to make.

Decision 5 sharpens this. k0s Autopilot — the upstream answer to in-place
Kubernetes upgrades — is disabled, correctly, because it mutates the k0s binary in
place and decision 3 says that binary is image content. So Corium disables the
mechanism and then does not replace it. What is left for an operator who wants a
different Kubernetes version on a running node is `cctl reset`, which throws the
node out of its cluster, or a full OS rebase to an image they may not want for any
other reason.

### What Talos does, and why it does not transpose

Talos separates `talosctl upgrade` from `talosctl upgrade-k8s`. The OS image
contains no Kubernetes version at all: the control plane runs as static pods from
registry images, the kubelet is a container image named per node, and an upgrade
rewrites image tags in the machine configuration. A support matrix bounds which
Kubernetes versions each Talos release accepts.

The shape is right. The mechanism does not transfer. k0s is a single
self-extracting executable — a binary with a ZIP payload appended, carrying
kubelet, containerd, runc, the API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd and
the CNI plugins — which stages its contents into `/var/lib/k0s/bin` on start
(`pkg/assets/stage.go`). There is no set of image tags to rewrite. Decoupling the
Kubernetes version from the OS version means decoupling *that file* from the OS
image, and nothing else.

### What the platform offers

- **systemd system extensions** merge `/usr` and `/opt` with an overlayfs, and the
  man page frames the use case as immutable system images explicitly. The merged
  `/usr` stays read-only. Extensions are searched for in `/etc/extensions/`,
  `/run/extensions/` and `/var/lib/extensions/`, the last of which systemd
  documents as the primary install location — and, on an OSTree system, the only
  writable one. `systemd-sysext.service` is ordered before `basic.target`, so an
  ordinary unit such as `k0scontroller.service` sees the merged tree without any
  work on our part.
  ([systemd-sysext(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/systemd-sysext.8.html))
- **Each extension declares what it fits.** `/usr/lib/extension-release.d/extension-release.<NAME>`
  must match the host's `ID`; if the extension sets `SYSEXT_LEVEL` that must
  match, and otherwise `VERSION_ID` must. This is the sharpest edge in the whole
  design and is treated as such below.
- **The pattern is established, but not for k0s.** Fedora's image-mode sysext
  project publishes `kubernetes-1.33` through `kubernetes-1.36`, and Flatcar's
  sysext-bakery publishes Kubernetes, containerd and Docker extensions with
  `systemd-sysupdate` metadata. Flatcar states plainly that updates are supported
  within a minor and never across one. Neither catalogue contains k0s, so Corium
  cannot consume this; it has to produce it.
  ([fedora-sysexts](https://fedora-sysexts.github.io/fedora/),
  [sysext-bakery](https://flatcar.github.io/sysext-bakery/kubernetes/))
- **k0s supports the swap.** `k0s stop`, replace the binary, `k0s start` is the
  documented upgrade path without Autopilot. The unit that `k0s install` writes
  bakes the absolute path of the binary into `ExecStart`, which would ordinarily
  make a swap a reinstall — but the path does not change here, because an
  extension overlays `/usr/bin/k0s` rather than replacing it somewhere else.
  ([k0s upgrade](https://docs.k0sproject.io/head/upgrade/))
- **k0s's version skew rules are stricter than upstream Kubernetes'.**
  Controllers must be within one minor of each other; a worker may be one minor
  older than the controllers and never newer; upgrades go one minor at a time,
  controllers first; and at bootstrap a worker must match its controllers exactly.
  ([version skew policy](https://docs.k0sproject.io/head/version-skew-policy/))

## Decision

**`/usr/bin/k0s` stops being image content and becomes a slot.** The path is
unchanged, and so is every caller of it — `internal/k0s.Binary` keeps its value.
What changes is who fills it.

### 1. The image still ships a k0s, and an extension overlays it

The OS image continues to install a pinned k0s at `/usr/bin/k0s` exactly as it
does today. That binary is the **floor**: the version a node runs when it has been
told nothing, when it cannot reach a mirror, or when its extension has stopped
matching.

This is the single most important part of the decision and it is deliberately
unglamorous. Shipping no k0s at all would be cleaner on paper and would make the
first-boot network reachability of a mirror load-bearing for a node's ability to
become a node — turning the sharpest failure mode (an extension that does not
load) from a degraded node into a dead one. It would also make this change
breaking for every node already in service. The floor costs one binary's worth of
image size and buys a node that always boots into *some* Kubernetes.

### 2. Extensions are signed OCI artefacts, pulled and verified like the OS

A k0s system extension is published as an OCI artefact, signed, and referenced by
digest. The node's existing container signing policy is the gate, the same one
`internal/upgrade/policy.go` already applies before `bootc` is allowed to move a
node to another OS image: an artefact is acceptable only if
`/etc/containers/policy.json` demands a signature for it.

This is reuse, not symmetry for its own sake. Corium already refuses to move a
node onto an unsigned OS image, and a file that becomes the kubelet and the API
server on that node deserves the same refusal. A bare URL and a checksum would
give integrity without provenance — it protects against corruption in transit,
not against the place the artefact came from, which is the distinction
`build/k0s.lock` already draws in its own header.

### 3. A new `corium.kubernetes:` block

```yaml
corium:
  kubernetes:
    version: v1.36.4+k0s.0
    mirror: registry.internal.example/corium/k0s
```

Both fields are optional, as decision 1's twenty-line constraint requires. No
`version` means the floor. `mirror` redirects the pull, which is how an air-gapped
site is served: point it at an internal registry rather than asking Corium for an
offline mode it would have to invent.

Validation is offline, per AGENTS §7: the version's syntax, its presence in the
support window the image was built with, and the skew rules are all checked
without a network call. Whether the artefact exists is a question for the pull.

### 4. The support window is three minors

An image supports the Kubernetes minor it ships as its floor and the two adjacent
ones — three in total, published as a matrix and stated in the docs. Three is
chosen from k0s's own skew rules rather than from taste: one minor at a time,
controllers first, workers no newer than controllers means a cluster mid-rollout
legitimately spans two minors, and a third gives an operator somewhere to go
without first taking an OS upgrade they did not ask for.

The window is a property of the OS image. Moving outside it is still a `bootc`
upgrade — the two axes are independent, not unbounded.

### 5. Matching is by `SYSEXT_LEVEL`, which Corium owns

An extension that pins `VERSION_ID` binds itself to a Fedora major. Since `/var`
is untouched by `bootc upgrade` by design, an extension in `/var/lib/extensions`
**survives an OS rebase and then silently stops matching** — a node that rebases
from Fedora 44 to 45 would come back on the floor version, or on nothing, having
been told nothing. Fedora's own sysext project lists this as a known issue.

So extensions declare a `SYSEXT_LEVEL` that Corium defines and versions
deliberately. The cost is honest and is accepted here: Corium takes ownership of
an ABI contract between its OS images and its k0s extensions, and bumping that
level is a reviewable event in the same way changing `build/k0s.lock` is today.

### 6. Day two: `kubernetes.version` joins ADR 8's safe subset, behind a skew gate

ADR 8 established that a bootstrapped node re-applies the fields whose reconciler
Corium already delegates to, and refuses everything that defines what the node is.
`kubernetes.version` joins `addons` and `k0s.patch` in the safe subset. It does
not define what the node *is* — the node is the same machine, in the same cluster,
under the same name and address, running a different build of the thing that
serves it.

It carries a constraint the other two do not, and `PlanReconcile` enforces it: a
change that violates k0s's skew rules is **refused with the rule named**, not
passed to k0s to discover at restart. Skipping a minor is the error an operator
actually makes, and the moment to say so is while nothing has moved.

Applying a version change is a bounded sequence the node performs on itself:
drain, `k0s stop`, swap the active extension, **clear `/var/lib/k0s/bin`**,
`k0s start`, uncordon. The purge is not tidiness. k0s skips re-staging its
embedded payload when the already-staged file's mtime equals the k0s executable's
and its size matches — and an EROFS extension built reproducibly has a normalised
mtime, so two versions can collide and leave a node running a stale kubelet
against a new control plane. The purge removes the possibility rather than
reasoning about when it can happen.

### 7. Ordering a rollout stays with the operator

`cctl` gains the verb; the daemon does not gain a rollout. A node knows only about
itself, and "controllers first, one at a time, then workers" is a statement about
the other nodes — exactly the division decision 11 and ADR 4 draw, and the one
`internal/cctl/rollout.go` already implements for OS upgrades.

### 8. Autopilot stays disabled

Decision 5 is not weakened by this record; it is what makes it coherent. Autopilot
was rejected because it mutates the binary in place behind the operator. Corium
now offers the capability Autopilot was wanted for — a Kubernetes version change
without a reset — as an explicit, operator-triggered, signed, drain-aware act. The
objection was never to in-place upgrades; it was to a controller performing them
unasked.

## Consequences

**Decision 4 is split, and should be read as two.** OS upgrades remain image-based
with atomic rollback, untouched. Kubernetes upgrades become their own axis with
their own verb. "One upgrade mechanism, one version axis, free rollback" was worth
stating while it held, and this record is where it stops holding. Rollback of a
Kubernetes version is no longer free: reverting to the previous extension is a
second forward operation, and k0s does not support downgrading a minor at all.
That has to be said plainly in the docs rather than left for an operator to
discover.

**Decision 3 is amended in letter, kept in spirit.** The binary is no longer
*image* content, but it is still read-only content from a signed, digest-pinned
artefact that nothing on the node writes to. "Immutability is the product" is not
traded away for a mutable `/usr/bin/k0s`; it is extended to cover a second
immutable source.

**Corium becomes a publisher of k0s artefacts.** Nobody publishes k0s system
extensions, so Corium builds, signs and hosts them. This is new supply-chain
surface and new release work — three minors, two architectures, signed and
published on their own cadence — and it is the largest single cost in this record.
It also means `build/k0s.lock` stops being a file about one version and becomes a
file about a window.

**Two version axes are two things to explain.** A support matrix has to exist, be
published, and be correct, and `cctl` has to answer "what Kubernetes am I
running, and what can I move to" without an operator cross-referencing a table.
The twenty-line constraint holds — both new fields are optional — but the concept
count went up by one, and that is a real cost to a project whose stated goal is
that a node be describable in twenty lines.

**A new failure mode needs to be visible.** An extension that stops matching does
not fail loudly; it simply does not merge, and the node comes back on the floor
version. Greenboot must check that the running k0s version is the declared one and
fail the boot if it is not, or the design's quietest error becomes its most common
support question.

**First boot can now depend on the network.** A node declaring a non-floor version
needs to reach its mirror. The floor keeps this from being fatal, but a node that
boots into 1.36 when its configuration said 1.37 has not done what it was asked,
and must say so rather than appear healthy.

## Alternatives considered

**Download the binary into `/var` at bootstrap.** The obvious implementation and
the reason to write this record instead. It puts a mutable, unsigned file on the
node's most critical path, gives up the read-only guarantee for the one binary
that most needs it, and reimplements — badly — the verification that
`policy.json` and the sysext machinery already provide. Cheap to build, expensive
to own.

**Build image variants: `corium:0.4.0-k8s1.33`, `-k8s1.34`, …** Preserves
decisions 3 and 4 completely, which is its appeal. Rejected because it does not
actually decouple the axes, it multiplies them: the OS × Kubernetes matrix is
every build, every sign, every publish and every test, and an operator changing
only the Kubernetes minor still takes a full OS rebase and a reboot to do it. It
moves the coupling into the tag and calls it a separation.

**Ship several k0s binaries inside `/usr` and select one at boot.** Keeps every
existing guarantee and needs no network at all, which is genuinely attractive.
Rejected because the window is still bounded by the image — reaching a fourth
minor is still an OS upgrade, so the coupling is loosened rather than broken —
and because three self-extracting k0s binaries is substantial dead weight in
every image, on every node, most of it never executed. It is the floor idea taken
to three floors, and the third floor does not pay for itself.

**bootc logically bound images.** The mechanism built for pinning content to an
OS image, so worth taking seriously. Rejected on a fact: LBIs deliver podman
containers, pulled at install and upgrade time, with no mechanism for landing a
file in `/usr/bin`. Reaching the binary would mean running a container to copy
its contents onto the host, which is a sysext with extra steps and no read-only
guarantee. The ecosystem is also still settling — Anaconda does not support them,
and image-builder has open issues where bound images fail against podman's
default store.

**Enable k0s Autopilot.** The upstream answer, available today, and it would close
the capability gap without Corium publishing anything. Rejected for the reason
decision 5 gives and this record keeps: it mutates `/usr/bin/k0s` on a running
node from a controller in the cluster, which is both a violation of the read-only
contract and a fleet-management posture decision 11 declines. A cluster resource
that rewrites the operating system is the wrong direction of control.

**Status quo.** Kept longer than it should have been, and worth stating why it
was defensible: one axis is genuinely simpler, and a project below 1.0 with a
small support surface can credibly say "take the image that has the Kubernetes you
want". It stops being defensible at the point where Corium has operators who need
a Fedora security fix without a Kubernetes minor bump, or a Kubernetes minor bump
without a Fedora rebase — both of which are ordinary, and neither of which the
image axis can express.
